utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, General. If you could kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Yes, Mr. Tieger. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours, and everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. If I could just intervene for a moment before Mr. Tieger begins his direct examination to put something on the record. Yesterday, during our interview of General Smith, it was indicated to us that he has given two statements previously to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and given testimony on one occasion in a preliminary examination in a case in Canada involving the hostage-taking that's the subject of Count 11, and I just wanted to indicate to the Trial Chamber that we think that the prior statements and testimony of a witness is an important tool for the Trial Chamber to use in assessing the credibility of a witness. And we're taking steps today to obtain that information from Canada, but we're not likely to receive it in time for General Smith to complete his testimony. And when we do get it, if we believe there's something in there that we thought should be brought to your attention, we'll take steps to do that, but I wanted to put it on the record now that that information is not in our possession at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. While I note your submission, I wish to say something about this matter, Mr. Karadzic, in general, of your efforts to obtain previous statements of testimony provided by General Smith in domestic proceedings before we begin to hear his evidence. The Chamber has previously advised you that there comes a point in every case where responsible Defence has to focus on the evidence and material before it and its position, rather than constantly searching for more information that may be of marginal importance. We understand that you feel that you must have it in your possession, every document bearing the slightest connection to your case, and that it may be a feature of your self-represented status that you do not fully appreciate that there is no Defence or Prosecution team at this Tribunal or in any domestic jurisdiction in the world that can have access to or to have analysed all such material. While at the same time complaining over and over again that you don't have sufficient resources to analyse the material disclosed to you by the Prosecution, Mr. Karadzic, you keep using the substantial resources that you have; so to speak, seven Defence team members remunerated by the Tribunal, in addition to your pro bono associates and interns, to pursue additional material that, in the end, may not be of much use to you. Therefore, I suggest that you take heed of this advice, speak to the experienced Defence counsel who are available to you, who know how the trial process runs, and think carefully about your strategy in this case. That said, sorry for the inconvenience, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say a word or two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you all. Your Excellency, I am very grateful for this well-intentioned advice. However, the position of this Defence is that it has to be different from the Defence cases in other trials. We saw how they concluded. Secondly, five team members are the number that I'm being remunerated for, but it's seven of them who are sharing this money. There are other things involved. I have to find documents that previous Defences had not found, and I have to complete the picture. Otherwise, it would be pointless for me to mount a defence if it were to be identical to the ones mounted before me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that you take into account what I have said to you. That said, Mr. Tieger, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Speaking of pragmatism, I just want to note that our LiveNote crashed, at least mine and Mr. Reid's, I believe, but we'll press on, nevertheless, and hopefully the technical people can offer some assistance and at a timely moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can were begin by asking to you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. My full name is Rupert Anthony Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, let me try to, however inadequately, briefly summarise some of your background. And, please -- I'll try to do that in a summary fashion. Please correct me if I've misstated any of the details. You graduated from Haileybury and the Imperial Service College in Sandhurst. You enlisted in the British Army in 1962, and you were commissioned into the Parachute Regiment in 1964. Your service and during the course of your career, and I believe that's approximately a 40-year career, has brought you to Africa, the Middle East, Europe, the Caribbean, and Asia. And just looking at your last 10 years of service, you were the general officer commanding the 1st Armoured Division from 1990 to 1992, which included the Gulf War. You also served as assistant chief of Defence Staff for Operations and Security from 1992 to 1994. I'll speak about that more in a moment. You commanded UNPROFOR, Bosnia-Herzegovina, during the year of 1995. You were general officer commanding in Northern Ireland from 1996 to 1998. You served as deputy supreme commander, Allied Powers Europe, from 1998 to 2001, and covered NATO's Balkan operations. And in January of 2002, you retired at the rank of general. Is that basically a correct summary, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, with two very minor points. I got further east than you described, to Australia and Malaysia, and the assistant chief of the Defence Staff job was in the Ministry of Defence in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, our focus during this proceeding will, of course, be your service as UNPROFOR commander during 1995, but I wanted to ask you if, prior to assuming those duties, you had the benefit of work that provided some knowledge and context of events in Bosnia and Herzegovina that preceded your assuming command.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. My responsibilities as the assistant chief of the Defence Staff for Operations and Security in the Ministry of Defence in London was essentially that of being the operations officer for the United Kingdom. And all the operations being conducted by the forces of the United Kingdom, the files, as it were, went over my desk, and so I had an understanding of the UN operations and the involvement of NATO in the Balkans from that capital's point of view and had been involved in some of the debate, and that was part of the decisions for the United Kingdom to be part of those operations and in the development of those operations up to the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I indicated earlier that your service as commander was during 1995. Do you recall precisely or approximately when you took command of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'll try and be precise. I think it was the 24th of January, but it was in January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, where were your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was that in a particular building or buildings?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the residency, it was called, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who was your predecessor, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: General Michael Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And your immediate superior, your military superior?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: General Janvier of the French Army, who was based in the UN headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was there also a UN civilian leadership to whom you reported?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. There was a -- there was the SRSG, Mr. Akashi, who was also up in Zagreb, and to him you went to the Department of Peacekeeping and the Secretary-General in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you indicated you were headquartered in Sarajevo, and so the UNPROFOR Bosnia-Herzegovina Command was there. Was there also a subordinate sector command located in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Based on a French Brigade headquarters, there was a Sector Sarajevo, and then there were two other sectors as well in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, General, let me take you back to your assumption of command in late January 1995 and ask you to briefly describe the circumstances and your primary responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: My -- I took over command not long after the signing of what had been -- what was called the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. This had been signed right at the end of 1994. And the immediate circumstances was one of setting out to implement the essence of this agreement or for the UN and UNPROFOR to play its part in implementing the essence of this agreement and the items in it. The -- my prior -- or the role of my command, the UNPROFOR, itself, in Bosnia-Herzegovina can be summarised, in that our purpose was to secure and support the UNHCR in the delivery of humanitarian aid and to play its part, the UN part, in the -- what had come to be called the safe areas and exclusion zone policy or resolutions. And -- but in the circumstances of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, it was the former one that was very much the primary concern when I took over. More immediately, on my own part, I wanted to get 'round my command and, of course, meet the Bosnian Serbs and the Federation parties and get to know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection, then, let me turn your attention quickly to a couple of exhibits reflecting meetings almost immediately after you arrived. And can I first have 65 ter 04754, and it would be page 11 of the English, please. And in this agenda book or diary, we see a notation for the 27th of January for 1200 hours: "General Smith." And let me show you next, and I'll advise the Court about both the nature and providence of this exhibit in a moment. The next exhibit will be 65 ter 04754 -- excuse me, P1487 and page 183. And, General, P1487 has been admitted into evidence as the note-books of General Mladic. Here, for the entry for the 27th of January, 1995, we see notes under the heading "Reception of General Smith." First entry: "He was greeted by Radovan." General, before I ask you about the nature of this meeting, let me ask you if the two notebook entries are consistent with your recollection of the timing of a meeting with General Mladic and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, this would connect with my memory, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to 65 ter 04754, that was a notebook that was seized from Mr. Karadzic's Belgrade flat at the time of his arrest. I don't believe there's any -- given the nature of the document, I don't believe there's any objection to its admission, but I would move it into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we hear from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably it would be wiser to admit it in its entirety --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- given the nature of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2242, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask something? There are a few volumes involved. Are all the diaries of my secretaries being admitted or just one particular volume for one particular year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How many volumes do you have, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, frankly, I don't know what this particular exhibit represents. I would presume that they are up-loaded as discreet volumes, given separate 65 ter numbers, and this one would, presumably, represent the agenda or notebook from that time. But we'd have no -- we can check, and of course we'd have no objection to -- since as the Court has indicated they're useful in their entirety, to doing so if this document doesn't represent the full duration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is minded to admit it in its entirety, but at this moment we'll admit this exhibit and we'll see what we can do later on. Yes, let's proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I -- may I just explain to the Chamber what this is all about? These are the diaries of my secretaries who recorded, who was visiting me, and how much time I was spending in the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, as we see from the notes of General Mladic, he has indications that you presented your team. You explained that your mission had two directions, including the delivery of aid to all those who need it, and to do the best you could to play your role in the UN for peace, et cetera; then raised questions about the shelling of Bihac and the exchange of liaison officers, one of whom, on the Bosnian Serb side, was in Gornji Vakuf. General, with respect to those particular comments attributed to you, are those in keeping with your recollection of the information you provided and -- well, let me ask you that first.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That would be the sort of thing that I would have discussed, I expect. I have no -- beyond the fact that this meeting took place, it was the first time we all met, I'm -- I probably did raise those things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated, General, that you wanted, from the outset, to meet with the parties to the conflict. Perhaps it's obvious, but can you tell us why you met immediately with Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic; that is, who they were and what their significance was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic was the president of the Bosnian Serbs, and General Mladic was the commander of their army. And I -- just as my predecessors had felt necessary, so did I, that if we didn't have a dialogue between us, the UN, and the commanders and political leaders of the factions in this conflict, then we were not going to achieve our objectives as the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll be touching on this issue during the course of your testimony in various ways, General, but briefly and generally, I wanted to ask you this: You indicated that you met with them because of your understanding about their leadership roles. During the course of your work as commander, your dealings with -- over time with General Mladic and President Karadzic, did you have the opportunity to observe the extent to which your understanding at the outset of their leadership roles was accurate?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It was quite plain to me that they were, as it were, who they said they were, that they were performing those roles, and that as -- and in establishing this dialogue, one's purpose is to understand the intentions and path that the various factions were setting out to conduct themselves into the future. And in doing that, one starts to form an opinion as to how well or effectively these leaders are performing that function, and I came to the judgement that both Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic were very clearly in command of what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you able to determine the extent to which they either worked together or separately toward the intentions and objectives that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: At this time or as the -- as the year developed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Over time, sir.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Over time. The -- they were clearly operating together. They were there along with Koljevic and Krajisnik, at the same table. They were all as one in the meeting. And, indeed, that was what -- how we were told by them, that they operated together as one. This you could see developing -- you could see examples of it as the year developed. There were occasions when you detected a degree of tension between the political and the military. I think we were detecting some in April. But there was little doubt in my mind, and it evaporated quite quickly, as to that they were not, as it were, joined at the hip as the Bosnian Serb leadership and they were conducting themselves on a single direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the existence of any tensions that you did observe strike you as unusual or noteworthy in the context of a political and military relationship?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there are always, speaking from my own experience, tension, not necessarily destructive tension, but, nevertheless, tension between political and military when you're conducting these major endeavours. The military are trying to turn a political intention into a military act, and the consequences of that military act may have political effects that were unwanted. So there's a constant tension between the two. So it's not surprising to me if you see this tension in existence. It's when it becomes destructive to that group of people that it matters. I never saw it reach that stage. When I saw tensions, I assumed that this was, as I've tried to describe, the normal, what you might expect from -- in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the military, itself, the -- that is, the Bosnian Serb Army, did you have an opportunity to observe the nature of its command structure and command-and-control relationships?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And, again, speaking from the impression formed over time, here was an army from -- in which orders were obeyed, in which instructions were -- if they were given at the top, you saw action being taken on them at the bottom. Equally, you could -- I mean, something could happen at the bottom and you could see the communications going to the top. And I had -- can give you one example. On one occasion, the -- in fact, when I was visiting Srebrenica, we got lost. We finished up at a check-point and were held at the check-point. My -- this was in Bosnian Serb territory. My liaison officer was able to go into the check-point, pick up the telephone, and talk directly to Mladic, who gave orders for us to be cleared to go through and down this route and rejoin the correct route.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, we'll be looking at a number of documents during the course of your testimony, and you may have an opportunity to amplify on some of the observations and experiences you just related in that regard. Let me turn our attention next to a meeting that took place with General Mladic again relatively shortly after your arrival, this one on the 14th of February, 1995, which is 65 ter 21988. And, General, let me -- you'll see the documentation to which your attention will be drawn on screen. Please feel free at any point, if you wish, to ask to have either a section --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It would be a great deal better if it was made a little larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you can control the scrolling down if you need to review the document.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Can I -- with this? What do I do, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you just ask the Registrar to do so.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: We can make it smaller. And you've gone -- that's about right, that's fine. And could we go down the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. General, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about some -- a couple of questions about some particular portions of the document. First, let me ask you at the outset if you recall, generally, what the focus of this meeting was.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I remember those issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the entry at paragraph 2: "The purpose of the meeting was to see how a cease-fire could be achieved in Bihac, how the clearances or humanitarian convoys could be freed up, and then whether a CJC in Bihac was a start. We emphasised the dire humanitarian situation in Bihac and the international profile which it was receiving. Mladic's response was to describe the imbalance of the system which, in his view, denied aid to the Bosnian Serb citizens but sent food and military supplies to the Muslim enclaves." Can you tell the Court, please, what your concern was at the time about the humanitarian convoys, the nature of the situation that prompted that concern, and the nature of the response you received from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't have a very clear recollection of the details of the situation around Bihac at the time, but it -- to some extent, it had been the poor relation of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. And the -- and the fighting in that area had either never really stopped or had flared up again, and I can't remember which it was, but there was a clear need to get some convoys of aid into the Bihac -- to the population in Bihac and to resupply the UN battalion that was there, which from my memory came from Bangladesh. The -- and that was -- it was the juxtaposition of all those events, the fighting, the resupply of the humanitarian aid, and the resupply of the UN battalion, that had, as it were, made this issue a big one in comparison to everything else at the time. The commentary of the exchange was that you see here a characteristic of these meetings, I will only do this if you do that; negotiation, as it were, against the previous agreement. And so you see that in this case with the, People have got to withdraw before I let anything in, and then you -- and you get this comparison that, If you're supplying those people, you must supply me. And we have this continuous fundamental point that keeps coming through is, if you like, the difference between impartiality and neutrality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection, if we can look quickly at paragraph 8 or point 8 of the document, which is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That reflects a complaint by Tolimir about reciprocal delivery, matching in quantity, and then a response that this was "not the basis for the UNHCR's well-proven assessment system, but he was adamant." First of all, very quickly, who was Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: He was -- he frequently -- he was a general. He was one of the chiefs of staff, if my memory serves me right, for security in the Bosnian Serb headquarters, and he frequently accompanied Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does the complaint that he registered and the response that he received reflect what you were trying to describe earlier?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, and it's a theme that runs through these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And because we may have occasion to address or rely upon this distinction, you mention the difference between impartiality and neutrality, perhaps you could amplify on that a bit in this context.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: This was how I understood it, or, rather, I still understand it and understood it at the time, and I would use an example which, from memory, I used at the time as well; that if I was a doctor in the British Army on operations, I would not be neutral. I would be a member of the British Army, and I would be wearing the uniform of the British Army. But if, in my dressing station, a casualty of the enemy was brought in along with a casualty from my own army, and the enemy casualty was much more severely injured than the soldier from my own army, then my duty, as a doctor, was to act impartially and to treat the enemy soldier not only with more medicine and so forth because his wounds and injuries needed it, but to treat him first because he was the more urgent case, and there I was behaving impartially. And I used that difference and that understanding in trying to explain the difference between the UN being neutral and the UN being impartial in these circumstances of Bosnia in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you distinguished -- or made a distinction between humanitarian aid to civilians and convoys that were resupplying UNPROFOR forces. Did both of those issues continue to be a source of concern for you during the course of your service and a source of tension or friction between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In Bihac or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Overall.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In Bihac, certainly. And overall, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn next, then, to P14 -- 01470, which reflects a meeting between yourself and -- or notes of a meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're minded to tender the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2243, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P01470, General, is a document, and if we turn the page, it is dated the 6th of March, 1995, and reflects a meeting between yourself and General Mladic on the 5th of March, 1995. And you can just take a glance at that. I'll direct your attention to certain portions of it. Turning your attention immediately to the first paragraph, it indicates, in the middle of -- again, it indicates General Tolimir's presence, as you noted earlier, and indicates, in the middle of the paragraph, that: "It was clear that there had been a high-level meeting at the resort over the weekend involving Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic and Mladic." And that: "Several officials from Belgrade were observed when you arrived, including one identified as Mr. Budimir Kosotic ..." And so on. We'll see a reference in the latter part of the document to a discussion with Professor Koljevic and, again, a reflection of major discussions before that meeting, but I wonder if you could indicate to the Court what you learned about a high-level meeting that had been conducted over the weekend at Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I have difficulty, in that I now know what happened, but my understanding -- I think my understanding at the time was that there had been this high-level meeting and that they had had it. It had been decided that the -- that the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement was breaking down and that they would now try and achieve the object intended for the Bosnian Serbs by force of arms, that they would be ready to fight to achieve their objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn you next to paragraph 3 of the meeting. There, it indicates that you questioned General Mladic on the reason for the up-surge in sniping attacks in Sarajevo. First of all, General, when you raised the issue of sniping attacks, what kind of -- sniping attacks on whom, by whom?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- again, I can't remember the details, but there had been, during the end of February - I couldn't tell you when it started - but an increase in sniping across the confrontation line between the defenders of Sarajevo and the Bosnian Serbs. The -- some of this was clearly, if you like, military in its -- it was soldier on soldier. Others was sniping of civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was your concern, in raising this with General Mladic, focused on one or the other --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I see, yes. No, the concern was focused on the -- on the latter, the sniping of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you make that clear to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think I must have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was General Mladic's response to you in -- when you raised your concerns about an up-surge in sniping attacks on civilians?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you -- you get the -- there were two things, and again this applies -- this is a frequent theme that runs through these exchanges. The response is that, We are doing it because they're doing it, and, secondly, And you're not stopping it. So I had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That indicates that: "The bulk of the meeting and evidently the main issue Mladic wished to discuss was the effect of sanctions on the Bosnian Serbs." And then there's a discussion about that. At the bottom of that first paragraph, before the subsections, it indicates: "General Mladic then threatened a blockade of all enclaves, including Sarajevo, if sanctions were not lifted." And then it indicates what you explained in response. Can you indicate to the Trial Chamber what the nature and significance of that exchange was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Although this didn't precisely distill in my mind at this stage, we're getting very close to the realisation that the enclaves, in which I included Sarajevo, was the -- going to be, as it were, the key to the -- what the Bosnian Serbs were going to be attending to in the immediate future, and that the -- they saw this as a way of bringing pressure upon us, the UN, and as a way of relieving pressure on themselves, both by punishing the United Nations and, therefore, the international community, who were sanctioning them, but also, as I came to realise within a few days of this, that this would be a way of freeing up their own forces and resources for their own operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to paragraph 6. That will be on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That indicates a discussion between you and Professor Koljevic, who arrived late, toward the end of the meeting, and who was extremely irritated and agitated about a letter that Mr. Karadzic had received from Mr. Akashi. What was the nature of -- or the cause of or focus of Koljevic's irritation? What did he say about it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: If I remember, the burden of the letter was about the delivery of the aid. But there was a paragraph in it drawing Karadzic's attention to the International Law on Non-Combatants, if I remember the bit correctly, and this had been interpreted as a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The document indicates that Koljevic said: "If he goes, we all go, and we don't mind how many we take with us." Was that, as you recall the discussion a reflection -- an accurate reflection of Koljevic's attitude toward what he considered the threat of war crimes trials for humanitarian abuses?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that I was talking to a man manifestly hung over, I can't remember more. I just took it at face value that that's what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we may, let's take a quick look at the letter that was the subject of Koljevic's ire. That would be 65 ter 01322. And if we could see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In this document, General, we see, and we can see on the next page, it's from Mr. Akashi, writing Dr. Karadzic, explaining that it's his solemn obligation to write on the subject of the highest humanitarian nature that has generated serious concern. And then it continues to describe the nature of the problem. As we see in the third paragraph: "The reports of the international humanitarian organisations and our own assessments depict a gruesome picture of complete lack of basic medicines, including insulin, cardiac drugs, anti-inflammatories, basic antibiotics, and even aspirin." It talks about the effects on the civilian population and, in particular, the most vulnerable groups of elderly and children. And if we could just continue to scroll down so we can see the signature page. That would be the next page, please. And if you look at the penultimate paragraph, indicating that: "The responsible authorities need to be reminded of the relevant provisions of Security Council Resolution 771 ..." And, in particular, the Geneva Conventions, and concludes that suspected violations of International Humanitarian Law are subject to investigation. Was that the paragraph that you understood Professor Koljevic --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it's that penultimate paragraph that I'm -- that I'm recalling, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this document could be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2244, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection, if we could perhaps look at 65 ter 13390.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, as we're able to see from the signature page, this is a letter from Mr. Karadzic to Mr. Akashi, responding to Mr. Akashi's letter of the 4th of March, which we just looked at. The second paragraph, as you can see, notes the language of the letter asserts that Mr. Akashi greatly exaggerates the difficulties concerning medical supply of the eastern enclaves; asserts that his information or "our information," as it says there, is that problems are not of that magnitude. And: "Where problems genuinely exist, we shall strive to eliminate them." And then it goes on, if you'll look at the letter, to raise a number of points, including the alleged violations of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. And then if we'll continue to the next page, please. Alleged arms supply to the Muslims, UNPROFOR's failure to face up to the real issues, and so on. First of all, General, let me ask you: In -- there are a number of issues raised in this letter, including the alleged double standards which the international community maintains. In light of your experience, is -- can you tell us whether that response by Dr. Karadzic to Mr. Akashi represented something unusual or whether it was -- it raised issues and was the kind of response you saw during the course of your service?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It's an example of what I was describing; that there is an acknowledgment that -- of the specific issue raised, and then you get the complaint that everyone else is -- You're not being fair, you're not treating everybody else the same as you're treating me, and, You -- if you like, You, UNPROFOR, are part of the problem, not part of the solution to this particular issue. And the major issue in this case, the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the document, Mr. Karadzic seems to assert some knowledge of what's happening in the enclaves. In your experience, did Mr. Karadzic claim, during your dealings with him, to know what was happening in the enclaves or to be unaware of what was happening in the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I was never in any doubt that he knew what was going on. What I'm -- I don't know at this range how I formed that opinion or if there was a particular case where he clearly knew the precise details of something, but I was quite confident he knew what was going on, or, put another way, could quickly find out if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2245, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, earlier you mentioned a visit to Srebrenica. Did you, in fact, visit the enclave in the early part of March 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Court, briefly, what you observed during the course of that visit?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. The visit to Srebrenica followed shortly after this -- the meeting in Jahorina we've just been talking about, and the journey to and from Srebrenica was very instructive to me, in that this was the first time, apart from driving up to Pale, that I had covered any appreciable length of Bosnian Serb territory, and I was very struck how empty it was of people or any signs of economic activity. I was also struck at -- on getting to Srebrenica and entering the pocket or enclave, that the isolation of the place and the palpable sense of this isolation within the enclave -- amongst the people within the enclave, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you able to observe or experience the -- any aspect of the control over the enclave exercised by the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. The -- there was a series of check-points around the enclave. There was evidence of defensive positions and so forth around the enclave, and there was a comprehensive search conducted of vehicles going into the enclave. There was a couple of humanitarian aid vehicles who were coming into the enclave at the same time as my vehicles, although we hadn't followed the same route, the same route to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And within the enclave, were you able to see the conditions that existed for the inhabitants and the conditions for UNPROFOR personnel?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. The -- it was very crowded. There was clearly a shortage of fuel. A lot of trees had been cut down for firewood. The levels of food and so forth were reported to me as being very low, and the -- and in particular, and this applied to the UN battalion, was the shortage of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, let me turn next to P00877 [Realtime transcript read in error "P8077"]. This document reflects a meeting between you and General Mladic on the 7th of March, 1995, which, as we can see from the notations in paragraph 4, took place after your visit to Srebrenica. Before scrolling down the page, if we could look at an entry on paragraph 2, the last sentence: "The major issues that emerged from the meeting were, firstly, a repetition of the linkage in the mind of the Bosnian Serbs between an UNPROFOR withdrawal from the UNPAs in Croatia and a demand that the UN withdraw from all enclaves in Bosnia, and, secondly, Mladic's explanation of his military concerns with the eastern enclaves." And if we could turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is P877 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I misspoke, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see how it's written. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, it indicates that General Mladic questioned you on the military situation and the activities of BiH within the Srebrenica pocket, and you reported that you had not seen any weapons within the town and that you had inspected the WCP. Again, although I believe the Court is aware, what is the WCP?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Weapons Collection Point. It's associated with the exclusion zone -- I'm not quite sure what I'd call it. Exclusion zone regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then the paragraph goes on to describe Mladic's request to you to order the withdrawal of UNPROFOR units from the area, his concern about a particular road, and his presentation of an interpretation of what the boundaries of the safe areas of Srebrenica, Gorazde and Zepa were or should be. And can you explain to the Court, please, what that was about?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- what he explained to me was that he had a different understanding as to what the safe area was within an enclave, that the boundaries of the enclave were not necessarily coterminous with the safe area, and we -- he, as I recall it, and I think that's what's written here, he got a map, and he explained that, in his view, when these things were agreed, this was the area, and he then drew a much smaller lozenge, as described here, a limited area in Srebrenica of about four and a half kilometres by a kilometre centred on the town, itself. That was his understanding, he said, of his -- of the safe area, and that's what had been agreed to. And that if he attacks, then he would respect that lozenge, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was your response to that, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, was to say that that wasn't how it was and that we'd actually -- the establishment of the enclaves had preceded the establishment of the safe area - he got things in the wrong order - and that the -- and that I wasn't about to move, which is what he wanted me to do, the UNOPs that were along the line of the existing confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, here in the middle of the -- approximately the middle of paragraph 5, there's a sentence that reads: "These concerns --" Referring to the concerns expressed above: "These concerns had led him to restrict the amount of food, medicine and fuel destined for the enclaves." General, by this time in early March, did you have any doubt about whether the restrictions on humanitarian aid or resupply for UNPROFOR were the result of local initiatives, or ad hoc determinations, or were centrally controlled?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: If not on this specific conversation, but it is about this point that I come to an understanding, which I subsequently referred to as my thesis, that not only were these punitive measures centrally directed and part of the overall scheme of the Bosnian Serbs, but we were also, the UN, in a situation which I came to call of the hostage and the shield. And this particular example was the decider, if you like, in me coming to that understanding, this particular trip into Srebrenica and coming out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, perhaps I could ask you to amplify on the concept of "hostage and shield."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, we -- let's use Srebrenica as an example. You -- the UN were there ostensibly to provide the humanitarian aid and to deter, by its presence, the assaults on the enclave, but we were -- in that role, we were, to some extent, a shield for the Bosnians on the inside, because they were able to then mount attacks out from the enclaves. And in the same token, we became a hostage to fortune. And you can see this thing here, that we stopped the -- the Serbs then stopped the aid coming in, the supplies to the unit, the UN unit in the enclave. And then you can find other examples where the situation is turned over and you are being used by the Bosnians as a hostage, as a -- to persuade the international community to take some action, and as a shield for taking that action by the Serbs because you're held there, and they -- you then become stuck in the middle again as one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, in connection with the understanding that you referred to about both central direction and part of the overall scheme with respect to the intentions toward the enclaves and restrictions of supplies, I'd like to direct your attention next to P838. And this exhibit reflects directive for Further Operations 7, and I'd like to direct your attention to further portions of that document. First, if we could turn to page 10, please, of the English. And directing your attention to the last paragraph, which begins speaking about enemy breakthroughs along selected operative-tactical lines should be prevented, and then continues about tying down as many enemy forces as possible, and then states: "... while in the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves. By planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity, with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." And before I solicit a comment about that, General, let me also turn your attention to paragraph 14 -- page 14, excuse me, and the last paragraph shown on screen, which is the third-to-last paragraph on that page, states that: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and the humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill, while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." General, if you can tell us whether those entries were consistent with your observations of the -- of how the enclaves and the issue of humanitarian assistance was dealt with, and your observations about the central direction of Bosnian Serb activities toward those issues.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'll take the first -- the last point first. It's clearly a central direction. Here is a high-level order being issued to carry this -- these actions out. I didn't recall the date or the -- who signed it when you put the first page up, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me go to page 15, the last page. There's the signature page and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's signed by the supreme commander, Mr. Karadzic, or, rather, Dr. Karadzic. And the -- and, secondly, that -- and page 10, the point on page 10 is -- I used the word at the time that the enclaves would be squeezed, and there is a paragraph describing squeezing and what you do to achieve squeezing of an enclave. And, indeed, that was starting to happen then, although one didn't see it in quite the way it was described and it was going to go, and then it was seen to continue during March and April and on into the year. The second thing you showed me on I think it was page 14 is, if you like, the orders to do the "hostage and shield" thing with UNPROFOR. We've got 14 back, yes. You see them here. You are to restrain, in so many words, by limiting the logistic support and so forth, on the one hand, but you're not to do it in such a way that we get ourselves into a position where we could be attacked. So we hide behind UNPROFOR, on the one hand, and we control UNPROFOR with the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had asked you earlier about the nature of the relationship between political and military structures, and the nature of the command-and-control relationship within the VRS. If I could quickly turn you to a couple of documents before the break. The first is 65 ter 03993. General, this is a document dated the 31st of March, 1995, very urgent, to the commands of the various corps, referring to a directive for Further Operations 7. And if we could continue down the page and turn the page, please. It goes on to describe the task of the VRS. And the next page, please. And if we can continue quickly to the signature page, please. And, again, in connection with that document as well, I wanted to also show you 65 ter 18968. That's also a document of the 31st of March, 1995, confirming receipt of the earlier document. General, can you tell us what those two documents, the first one signed by General Mladic, referring to the earlier Directive 7, and the Zivanovic receipt, sent to the Main Staff, of Mladic's 31 March directive?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- as I've understood, the three documents that we've seen, you see the political direction being matched by the military direction and then starting to cascade down the military chain of command. And in this case, we have the next level, the Drina Corps, receiving their copy. And there, I could recognise bits from the very first document appearing in the -- in the second, in its -- in the intent and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could tender those two documents, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P2246 and P2247 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, noting the time, it probably wouldn't be prudent to move to another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time to take a break. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, in connection with some of your earlier observations concerning orders, and beginning at the top, going to the bottom, reporting from the bottom to the top and so on, I wanted to show you a series of documents and ask you about those. And perhaps it's most useful if I show them to you one after another before attempting to elicit any comment. So if we could first turn to 65 ter 01326. Let's try, instead, 19008. General, this is a document dated the 26th of March, 1995, signed by Mr. Karadzic, and ordering, as we see if we scroll down, the "mobilisation of the complete human and material resources of Republika Srpska in order to finally crush and defeat the enemy." And if we could next turn to 65 ter 0315. I'm sorry if I misspoke. It was 06315. And if we could scroll down. This is a document dated the 28th of March, 1995, ordering the mobilisation of the entire manpower and material potential of Republika Srpska, with the objective of ultimately crushing and defeating the enemy. And if we could turn to the signature page, please. And that's issued by General Mladic. And next, 65 ter 13449. It's a document with two dates on it, the 27th of March and the 28th of March. Scrolling down, please: "We have received a document from the Main Staff ...," it reads, and then continues about receiving an order from the supreme commander, and ordering, therefore -- and containing the order to mobilise that we saw earlier from Dr. Karadzic: "With regard to the foregoing," it states at the bottom of the page and on the screen: "The commands and units of the Drina Corps shall continue to carry out combat assignments as set out in the previously received orders and will organise the admission and assignment into units of the additionally mobilised men." And if we could turn to the signature page of that document, please. And it's signed by General Zivanovic. And, finally, 65 ter 13439. It's from the Command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, dated March 29th, 1995, referring to the delivery of the order of the president of Republika Srpska on the mobilisation of the entire human and material resources, et cetera, and states that: "Through the Drina Corps Command, we have received an order of the president of Republika Srpska ...," et cetera. Referring in the first paragraph of what is ordered, that is: "I hereby order," it states, "the mobilisation of the entire human and material resources ...," et cetera. And the signature page, please. And that's signed by Major Rajko Kusic, commander. General, having seen those documents, can you tell us if that's consistent with your observations of the relationship between the political and military authorities, the command and control of the VRS, and your observations of the movement toward the implementation of the achievement of intentions via military means at that time of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It's a good example of what I talked about the political and military being joined at the hip. It is a -- although I wasn't aware that this was going on in this way at the time, you -- it gives an explanation as to why the -- you got the same political message, as it were, at a number of levels of command at the same time, because, of course, they were all being informed directly of the political setting of their military acts down the military chain of command by this sort of cascade of instructions. And, yes, here you see what I alluded to earlier, that they'd reached a decision in -- at the time of that meeting in Jahorina about a month before this, and here you see this total effort being prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could refer your attention -- Sorry, Your Honour. I'd like to move those documents into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit these four documents, but I'm wondering if there's a typo, in terms of date. I'm wondering how the Drina Corps document could be dated as the 27th, while the Main Staff document was dated as 28th of March. I checked the B/C/S version of the Main Staff. It was maybe the 26th. Could you check it right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will do so, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The four documents will be Exhibits P2248 through P2251.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And similarly, General, I wanted to show you three additional documents. The first is 65 ter 8961. That's not it. If that could be removed from the screen, please. It would be 18961. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, this is a document dated the 29th of March, 1995, an order issued by the president of the republic, Dr. Karadzic, and it calls for the setting up of ambushes immediately along the possible axes of withdrawal of units, and increasing the number of patrols controlling the area referred to above. And if we could next see 65 ter 07004.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, just one observation, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am afraid that this is expert based. It's not factual testimony. However, if the Trial Chamber allows this, I hope that we are allowed to do the same thing when we question our own witnesses, because the witness does not actually know about these documents. He is giving an ad hoc interpretation, and the distinguished Mr. Tieger is bordering on leading questions now. And the witness is speaking about documents that he is not aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I disagree, Mr. Karadzic. The witness was the commander of the UNPROFOR Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and he's testifying about his understanding, his understanding about these documents. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This document, General, is dated the 30th of March, 1995. And if we scroll down, it's to the Drina Corps commands. It refers to similar information. It refers to the order that we saw a moment ago, and then continues without stating -- if we could continue to the bottom of the page -- to the next page, please. It continues to issue orders -- or a series of instructions in reference to that order. And one more, please, and that would be 65 ter 08162. I believe we saw the previous order was to the Drina Corps Command. This is the Drina Corps Command document, dated the 30th of March, 1995. And if we scroll down to the next -- go to the next page, please. Again, at the top of the page, reference to the order of the president of the 29th of March, and ordering, among other things, in paragraph 2, the setting of ambushes in a particular sector. And again, General, I'd ask you if this series of orders is consistent with your observation of the relationship between the political and military authorities and the command-and-control structure.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And you can see, in the first one, that it's also directed to the Ministry of the Interior, and you can then see the liaison being required at the next level down the chain of command on the military orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender those documents for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit those three documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P2252 through P2254, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I'd like to return to some of the meetings that were taking place during that period. And in that connection, I'd like to bring on screen 65 ter 13126. And if we could go to the next page, please. This is a meeting that was conducted with Bosnian government officials. If we go quickly to the -- through the document, I wanted to indicate to you I don't believe there's a signature page, and I'll be asking you who the "I" is in this document. Scroll down to the bottom, please. And if we could then return to the previous page. I'm sorry, the first page, please. Looking at the first paragraph, General, and the date of the meeting, and you're certainly welcome to look at any other portion of the document for purposes of this question or any other, this indicates that the protagonist of this note was met first with Minister Muratovic and General Delic, was accompanied by the force commander, et cetera, and that his arrival in Sarajevo was marred by the apparent killing of two young girls, the closure of the blue routes across the Sarajevo Airport, et cetera, and the fact that his aircraft was hit by machine-gun fire as it taxied after landing in Sarajevo. The purpose of the meeting was in connection with the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, and that he would be travelling to Pale the next day to likewise encourage Serb authorities there. Do you know who this refers to?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think the "I" is Mr. Akashi. It certainly isn't me, because I'm commander of BHC, and it's -- nor is it my delegate in Bosnia and my political adviser. So I think it's Mr. Akashi, and he would refer to his aeroplane -- it was his. And we were all in it when it was hit by machine-gun fire that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And since that incident came up in connection with identifying who was being referred to in that document, can you tell us, quickly, what that incident was about and who fired on Akashi's plane?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The firing was by the Bosnian Serbs, and my -- I recall that Mladic acknowledged as much subsequently. And my recollection was that it was actually -- we were in the process of landing, as opposed to taxiing, when a round or two of a burst of fire went through the back end of the aircraft, and one round, at least, was found in -- embedded in someone's baggage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, there is a reference to "the shelling of Sarajevo last night." And if we could turn to paragraph 4. We see references to both the killing of the two young girls referred to earlier in the document and to the fact later in the paragraph, that at a press conference: "I," that is Akashi, as you've identified him, "condemned the shelling and sniping incidents and also successfully urged Minister Muratovic to condemn the killing of the two young girls." And there's also reference to the issue of the closure and the hoped-for reopening of the blue routes. Do you recall either these particular incidents of shelling and sniping referred to in this document or the general occurrence of shelling and sniping on Sarajevo during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: As we -- in an earlier question, you asked me about sniping in February. There was a general increase in the incident rate of shelling and sniping that continued. And I've forgotten the date of this meeting, but we're at the end of -- we're about the middle of March, if I remember the front page or the date on this. And there was this incident of these two girls being killed by sniper fire, and very shortly after that, as I remember it, the blue routes were shut and there was an increase in shelling and so on, and that's what we're referring to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to make it completely clear: The two girls who were killed by sniper fire, were those girls Bosnian Serb or Bosnian Muslim victims?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: They were -- the victims were Bosnian Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you refer to the blue routes being shut and an increase in shelling, who shut the blue routes and who engaged in the shelling?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs' reaction was the shutting the routes and the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was that shelling a shelling of military targets or civilian areas?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: A bit of both, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2255, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, for further clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go on: General, do you, by any chance, know the nature of this document? Can we see the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In e-court, did we have another page? This is page 2 of a document of eight pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that it has been missing, the cover sheet, for some -- since we received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I was about to ask whether it is a kind of correspondence. It looks like a letter, if you see the previous page. But if -- I'm fine. Let us proceed, because we have heard already the witness cannot help us in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The most amplification I can offer at this point, Your Honour, is this -- we received this document attached to a cover sheet which disseminated the document, but not a separate cover sheet for this -- that referred to this document in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you referred to the general increase in the incident rate of shelling and sniping that continued during this period of time, and I wanted to ask you whether -- first of all, what was the object of that shelling and sniping, military targets, civilian -- civilian areas? And, secondly, who was engaged in the shelling and sniping that was increasing?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring to Sarajevo here, the -- where I have slightly more of a memory, if only because I was in Sarajevo. You could -- and, again, the -- this is -- both sniping and shelling fell into two piles, if you like, of incidents. There were those that were clearly involved by location and target along the front-line or the confrontation line, and then there were those that occurred along particular roads. There was one in Sarajevo - known as Sniper Alley - where we -- where civilian movement took place, but it was in view -- or at stretches of that road or area were in view of the confrontation line, and you got sniping in those sorts of places. And we -- as I remember it, we had a soldier killed who was putting up, I say, containers in order to screen the -- this sort of area from view of the -- of the confrontation line. The shelling also occurred in those two groups of incidents. There, that was clearly related to the confrontation line, and then that that fell in amongst the rear areas, amongst the civilian population, and that tended to be -- appeared to be, at least, random and tended to occur on an intermittent basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The shelling of civilian areas, who was that -- who was doing that shelling?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The bulk of the shelling was coming -- both mortar fire and artillery fire was into Sarajevo, into the Bosnian-held bit of Sarajevo itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And by --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: -- from the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the course of your service as commander, were you able to identify the effect or objectives of shelling civilian areas?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The objective, that appeared to me to be to harass the population at large. The -- there was no specific target and there was no -- and as I say, these events occurred, as it were, randomly. You couldn't see them being connected to an event that was actually happening on the ground where this shell or shells landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does the random nature that you just described advance or under-cut the attempt that you mentioned, to harass the population?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It is, to put it mildly, extremely wearing to live in circumstances where you don't know where the next shell is landing and you don't know when it's going to land, so you spend all the time waiting for this bang to occur. It's very exhausting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to 65 ter 13126. And if we could continue, this may reflect the meetings with -- that were referred to earlier, the intended meetings with the Bosnian Serb officials. I'm sorry. We can continue on to the next page, please, to -- and further. And continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, here we see a meeting of the 14th of March, 1995, and the indication, that Mr. Akashi has travelled to Pale, where he met with Bosnian Serb leaders, including Dr. Karadzic, General Mladic, Mr. Krajisnik and Professor Koljevic, again accompanied by the force commander and by his delegate in Bosnia. And it referred, at the outset, to the relatively combative mood of the Serb leadership. And if we could turn to paragraph 6. There, it is a reference to the subject of freedom of movement, particularly with regard to the delivery of humanitarian assistance, and General Mladic's insistence on absolute parity between what was delivered to the Bosnian Serbs and what was delivered to the enclaves, a reference to sanctions. And, finally, toward the bottom of the paragraph, the subject of the blue routes is raised with Mr. Karadzic informing Mr. Akashi that his authorities had previously communicated to the Bosnian government the Serb position, that they would close the routes for one month for every Serb that was killed by sniping in the Sarajevo area, a position from which it was impossible to dissuade them. General, if I could ask for your comment, please, about that particular meeting and where it fit into the issues with respect to humanitarian assistance, freedom of movement, and the general objectives that you've outlined.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: This meeting was part, as you can see, of a whole series being conducted by Mr. Akashi and continued into other subsequent meetings to try and get the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement back on track, but in each case you just -- you come back down to the specifics of a particular case where -- and every -- so you can see you're going from blue routes around Sarajevo to Bihac, and specific details, as opposed to dealing with the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement as a whole. And the particular attempt that we're trying to do is to get the Joint Commission up and running so that some of these particular issues could be dealt with in detail in such a commission, rather than preventing all progress in the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement from taking place. The -- and, again, you get this continuing demand that, If X is provided with stuff, then I must be provided with the same amount of stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the reference by Mr. Karadzic to the closure of the blue routes, in response to the sniping killing of a Serb, indicate to you anything about the awareness of the political or military leadership about events in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- I mean, that was all the effect of -- the killing of the two girls had become a political issue, if you like, the day, almost as if it occurred, so it was such a shocking event, as it were, and this -- that didn't surprise me in the reference there to the -- to the closing of the blue routes. All of that was connected with the -- with the snipers killing the two girls.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in connection with that, if I could quickly show you two documents. The first is P879. This is a Main Staff -- VRS Main Staff document, dated March 11th. And if we could go to the next page, please, to paragraph 6. I guess that would be on the following page. And if we look at paragraph, it looks like it would be, 6(C) (II), or, sorry, that would be item 2, which states: "Due to sniper fire and the death of the two girls, any movement of humanitarian organisations and convoys is prohibited until further notice." And if we could turn next to 65 ter 12301. This is a Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command document, dated the 12th of March, 1995. And if we could go to paragraph 3. Again, the situation in the territory, the order about closing of: "... the blue roads has been delivered or issued to the units, and it is being implemented in practice."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, were these -- these two documents, do they reflect events consistent with your observations at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender the second document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2256, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to 65 ter 10616. This is a weekly situation report for the period 12 through 18th of March, 1995. And if we could turn to paragraph 3, please, which states: "Bosnian Serb leaders, including Karadzic and Mladic, in a meeting with Mr. Akashi in Pale on 12 March, also made clear their intention to pursue their objectives through military means if they were not able to achieve them at the negotiating table. Based on recent developments, there is no reason to believe that the Serbs are any closer than in the past to attaining their objectives through negotiations." And if we could turn to paragraph 7 quickly. And that reflects, again, the closure of the blue routes and the Bosnian Serb pledge to keep them closed, based on the killing of -- the sniping killing. And, finally, if we could turn to paragraph 10, which indicates that: "The situation in the eastern enclaves has not improved. UNPROFOR is having grave difficulty in obtaining clearance for resupply convoys, particularly for fuel. UNPROFOR troops in Zepa currently have no fuel stocks left; those in Gorazde and Srebrenica are on the verge of running out."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, I apologise for moving quickly and drawing your attention to three different items, but first, as a general matter: Do -- were the circumstances outlined in this document consistent with your understanding and observations at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2257, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like next to turn quickly to 65 ter 01684. And I just wanted to show you a couple of additional March-related documents. This is one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, this is a document from the Office of Civil Affairs Command, Sarajevo, dated the 27th of March, 1995. It refers to a meeting in Pale on the 25th of March that you and "I" -- presumably that's the -- I don't know if that's the releasing officer or someone else mentioned in the cover sheet, had a meeting with Professor Koljevic and Jovan Zametica, during which Koljevic stated that the Serb intention was now to pursue an end to the war through military means, and it contains further elucidation of that discussion, including, at the end of paragraph 2, the direct question: "Now, although you wish to have a cessation of hostilities and a peace plan, you wish to achieve a cessation of hostilities by fighting?" "Koljevic: Yes, exactly." "Smith: So, Enrique's and my role is thus extremely limited. If I understand you, you are now set on a course to fight to a conclusion." "Koljevic: Yes, absolutely." And at the end of paragraph 3, Professor Koljevic, referring to the fact that: "It is quite obvious, from the military point of view, that time does not favour the Serbs." In paragraph 4, your serious and formal protest for an artillery attack that day by the VRS or the BSA, the Bosnian Serb Army, from within Gorazde Exclusion Zone; a reference to the fact that this could hardly be in the Bosnian Serbs' interest, and Koljevic asserting that he believed that "we know our interests best." And finally in paragraph 5, a further reflect of, what is referring to here as: "The continued commitment by Pale to the closure of the blue routes for 30 days for every Serb killed by sniping in Sarajevo." General, is that an accurate account of that meeting, is it consistent with your recollection of events at the time, and do you have any additional comment about the positions taken by Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It fits with my recollection. You will see - I think it's in paragraph 3 - that it is -- Enrique is the "I." Or somewhere in there, I'm quoted and saying in -- that Enrique and I, What am I to do about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it certainly seems clear enough on the cover page as I look at it now to Mr. Akashi from Enrique --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: This -- as I said before, that my thesis had started to form at the end of February/beginning of March, and here was added evidence that only confirmed me in my view that we were heading down this direction in -- of war. And to try and resolve this matter by force of arms was the determination of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: And the other point was, of course, we've just had this Bosnian -- these, if I recall, two attacks, one in the north-east, if I recall correctly, and the other to the west, which had been fairly substantial attacks by the Bosnian Army, and they'd had some success against the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In paragraph 4, you're recorded as indicating that a serious -- or a formal protest would ensue for an artillery attack. I wanted to look quickly at 65 ter 01326. The cover page indicates a document from you, dated 25 March 1995. The subject is: "Protest letter - Gorazde. Letter sent to General Mladic." And if we could turn the page. It indicates that you write to express your profound concern over the actions of General Mladic's army, and then refer to an incident in Gorazde where initial reports indicate that seven civilians were severely injured, and the second paragraph indicating a similar attack around the same time in Mostar, where a further six civilians were wounded and one child killed. Is this document -- and there's a copy to Professor Koljevic at the bottom. Was this the protest referred to in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
